opus-5.5.text:
I think the boundary keeps moving, and the interesting part is which direction it moves.

For a long time we defined human capability by what machines couldn't do: chess, then Go, then natural language, then coding. Each time AI crossed one of those lines, people said, "Well, that wasn't real intelligence anyway." I've seen that firsthand working on Go. Before AlphaGo, many people thought Go was a deep test of human intuition. Afterward, top players began studying AI moves and discovered ideas no human had explored in centuries. So the boundary didn't shrink. It shifted. Humans became stronger by learning from the machine.

I expect that pattern to spread to many fields. When large models can draft code, write reports, or do routine analysis, raw execution stops being the differentiator. What matters more is asking the right question, setting the goal, judging whether an answer is actually good, and taking responsibility for the decision. In a sense, AI pushes humans up the abstraction ladder: less "how do I do this," more "what should be done, and why."

There's also a subtler point. Current models are trained mostly on data humans have already produced, so they're very good at interpolating within what we collectively know. Truly new insight, the kind that changes how we see a problem, is still hard for them. That's one reason I care about understanding *how* these models learn, not just scaling them. If we understand the mechanism, we can see more clearly where their limits are and where humans still add something unique.

My view is that the real human capability boundary isn't a fixed list of skills. It's our ability to keep redefining what's worth doing. AI will absorb many tasks we once considered uniquely human, and that's fine. The people who thrive will treat it as an amplifier: someone with ideas and taste can now accomplish what used to take a whole team. So I'm actually optimistic. The boundary of what one person can achieve is about to get much larger.

r001.rationale: The response says that after AI crossed a capability line, the boundary shifted and humans became stronger by learning from the machine.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the boundary keeps moving, and it moves in ways that surprise me.

If you'd asked me ten years ago, I would have described the boundary in terms of specific tasks. Go was on the other side of it. Then it wasn't. Protein folding, competitive programming, writing a coherent essay. Each of those felt like a landmark, and each one got crossed faster than most of us predicted. So the first thing I've learned is to stop defining the boundary by tasks, because tasks are exactly what these systems are good at absorbing.

What I now think about instead is something more like the structure of a problem. Where does the problem come from? Who decided it was worth solving? What counts as a good answer? A lot of what we used to call intelligence was really execution: given a well-posed problem, find the solution. Chess, math olympiad questions, even much of coding. AI is going to eat most of that. I don't say that with anxiety, I say it as a research reality. Search plus learning plus scale is a very powerful combination, and when the objective is clear, it works.

The part I'm genuinely uncertain about is the upstream side. Noticing that something is a problem at all. Deciding that a weird anomaly is interesting rather than noise. Taste, basically. When I look at how I actually do research, the hard moment is rarely the proof. It's the week before, when I'm staring at something and I can't articulate why it bothers me. I don't fully understand what's happening in my own head there, and that makes it hard for me to say whether a model can do it or not.

So my honest expectation is that the human capability boundary is going to shift from "doing" toward "choosing." That sounds comforting, but I want to be careful, because I also think the systems will start participating in the choosing. They already propose hypotheses. They already notice patterns I missed. So the boundary is less a wall and more a collaboration frontier that keeps getting renegotiated.

And then there's the part that I think people under-discuss: the boundary isn't fixed on the human side either. Humans with these tools are a different kind of thinker than humans without them. A graduate student today can test ideas in an afternoon that would have taken me a semester. So when we ask what humans can do, we have to ask which humans, with what tools, at what point in time. I expect the ceiling of what one person can accomplish to go up dramatically, even as a lot of the individual skills we used to be proud of become less special.

If I had to compress it: I expect AI to make the question "what can humans do" less interesting, and the question "what do humans want to do, and why" much more interesting. That second question is where I think the real frontier is going to live for a while.

r001.rationale: The response says AI has crossed former human capability landmarks such as Go and protein folding, and describes the capability boundary as moving as a result.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will keep changing our understanding of what is uniquely human. When a machine cannot do something, we tend to say, “That requires intelligence.” Once it can do it, we say, “Well, perhaps that was just computation.” So the boundary moves, but our definition moves with it.

I would distinguish between doing a task and deciding what task is worth doing. AI may become very good at solving a problem with a clear objective. But in real life, often the difficult part is figuring out what you want, which constraints matter, and whether the result actually helps someone. AI can help with those questions too, but we still have to make choices and take responsibility for them.

So I don’t see the human capability boundary as a fixed line that AI approaches. The tools themselves expand what people can do. Something that previously required a large team might become accessible to one person. That changes which abilities matter: less emphasis on executing every step yourself, and more on asking useful questions, judging results, and connecting them to experience.

And I would be cautious about declaring any particular capability permanently beyond AI. We should leave room to be surprised.

r001.rationale: The response says the perceived boundary moves when machines acquire abilities people had called intelligent, but it does not clearly state that AI surpassing humanity’s previous best performance shifts that boundary upward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that boundary will keep moving. When AI becomes good at something we used to regard as uniquely human, we have to reconsider what the underlying capability actually is. Is it remembering a lot of information? Recognizing patterns? Or deciding which problem is worth solving in the first place?

But I wouldn’t think of it only as a competition between humans and machines. With better tools, an individual can explore ideas, write code, or understand a new subject much faster. So AI changes both the boundary of what machines can do and the boundary of what a person can do with their help.

The difficult part is that generating an answer and judging whether it is a good answer are different things. As generation becomes cheaper, judgment becomes more important: asking the right questions, checking assumptions, and deciding what outcome we actually want. I expect those responsibilities to change too, so I’m hesitant to draw a permanent line and say, ‘Everything on this side will always belong to humans.’

r001.rationale: The response says the boundary will keep moving as AI becomes good at tasks once seen as uniquely human, but it does not state that AI will surpass humanity’s previous best performance or that this will shift the perceived human capability boundary upward.
